 Early voting turnout surges across North Carolina 
 By Michael Perchick Monday, October 19, 2026 10:51PM 
 NC voters are heading to the polls at a pace well ahead of the last midterm election. RALEIGH, N.C. (WTVD) -- North Carolina voters are heading to the polls at a pace well ahead of the last midterm election, as national political figures descend on the state, and campaigns intensify their efforts to drive turnout.
 Through Sunday, 525,970 ballots had been cast statewide, an increase of more than 37% compared with the same point in the 2022 midterms.
 "These numbers are really set to break some records," said Dr. Michael Bitzer, a political science professor at Catawba College.
 At the Cary Senior Center on Monday, voters lined up outside to cast their ballots and cited a variety of issues motivating their decisions.
 "I think a lot of people want to see change right now," said voter Elizabeth Ballinger.
 Wake County led the state in both in-person early voting and total votes cast, followed by Mecklenburg, Durham, Guilford, and Buncombe counties.
 "I always like someone who votes for the environment. Someone who is interested in giving teachers higher pay, who wants to help with housing and medical expenses," said Ballinger.
 "Taxes are the main thing. What we tax and how we tax," fellow voter Arthur Miree said.
 Turnout figures thus far show registered Democrats have cast 240,206 ballots thus far, comprising 45.67% of all turnout. That's followed by unaffiliated (181,809 votes, 34.57% of turnout), Republican (102,845 votes, 19.55% of turnout), Libertarian (940 votes, .18% of turnout), and Green (170 votes, 0.03% of turnout).
 The gap comes despite unaffiliated voters making up the largest proportion of voters, with Democratic and Republican registration figures roughly even.
 "(Public opinion polling in the state) shows typically, if somebody identifies as a Democrat, 90% of the time they're voting Democratic. If you're a Republican, 90% of the time you're going to vote Republican. Unaffiliated within the polling numbers that I've seen are tending to break much more heavily towards Roy Cooper over Michael Whatley. And that is not surprising in this kind of an environment. If independents are indeed truly the unaffiliated voters, the likely bulk of the unaffiliated vote right now is going to Roy Cooper simply because of energy and enthusiasm dynamics," Bitzer said.
 Wake County Democratic Party Chair Wesley Knott said Democrats are cautioning supporters against placing too much confidence in polling showing Cooper ahead of Republican Whatley.
 "We're focused on making sure that folks know that you shouldn't rely on polling, that we have to turn out in massive numbers to win," Knott said.
 Wake County Republican Party Chair Sandy Joiner said Republicans are also seeing significant interest in the Senate contest.
 "We probably get about 10-20 people per day asking about Whatley," Joiner said. "We have Whatley signs. Whatley has been all over the state speaking. I believe he's got a strong showing," said Joiner.
 Both Knott and Joiner discussed key issues behind turnout.

 "Whether it is chaotic tariffs that raise prices for everything, war with Iran that is raising prices at the pump, (voters) are looking for change. I think people understand who controls Washington, D.C., who runs the legislature in North Carolina, and I think we have a real opportunity for change in this election cycle," Knott said.
 Joiner said, "We've had a lot of questions about lowering taxes, about the amendments and the bonds, and a lot of questions about school board. And, you know, what's going on with the schools in Wake County and the fact that a lot of the money has been spent and the schools are having a hard time just keeping up."
 National figures make their pitches
 North Carolina's political importance is also evident in the number of prominent national figures campaigning in the state.
 Vice President JD Vance visited western North Carolina on Monday to campaign for Republicans, while President Donald Trump is scheduled to hold a rally in Greenville on Tuesday. The visits follow a Triangle appearance last week by Democratic U.S. Sen. Raphael Warnock of Georgia.
 "Just the two of them, President Trump and Vice President Vance coming to North Carolina just shows how important North Carolina is," Joiner said.
 Knott said Democrats are similarly looking for surrogates who can energize their supporters.
 "From the Democratic side, we want to bring in anybody that can excite our voters and help make them tune in to what is happening," Knott said. "I'm sure the folks on the other side of the aisle are doing the same."
 Bitzer said those visits can serve a purpose beyond helping candidates on the ballot this year, as politicians potentially eyeing future campaigns build relationships in battleground states.
 "This is a classic component of any midterm election, particularly before an open-seat presidential election," Bitzer said. "The wannabe candidates for two years from now are really kind of road testing and going to various battleground districts and states to lend their support, to lend their assistance, to try and get their candidates elected, who can then turn around if they were successful and say, 'Hey, remember when I came to North Carolina in 2026 and helped you get elected as a US senator or US member of the House of Representatives or whatever office? I'm now back, and I'd like to have your support for my presidential bid.' This is a classic midterm dynamic that we see as an undercurrent, but it pays dividends come the next presidential primary contest."
